title: Workshop I — Ingestion
intro: You are a data engineer at RetailHub. Load raw customer (CSV) and order (JSON) files, transform them and write a Bronze Delta table with load metadata. Pick your track at the top: **SQL** or **PySpark**; you can switch at any time. Every step is completed here: fill in the blanks, put the blocks in order or match the pairs, and the step turns green when your answer is right. Running the code is optional: the **Notebook (optional)** section of a step has the completed code for the notebook `WORKSHOP_ingestion`, and you can click **Check on data** to test your result on real data. Optional steps can be skipped.

steps.title: The building blocks of this workshop
steps.explain: This workshop uses a small set of building blocks again and again: reading files, casting types, conditions, aggregates and filters. Match each expression with what it does; you will use all of them in the next steps.

pairs.right: CASE WHEN cond THEN 'New' ELSE 'Loyal' END

hints: Read the PySpark side as SQL: the function name usually stays the same (`year` → `year`, `count` → `COUNT`).
`.alias(...)` is SQL `AS`, `.otherwise(...)` is `ELSE`, and `.filter(...)` becomes a `WHERE` clause.

Pairs: `F.col("city")` → `city`; `F.year(...)` → `year(registration_date)`; `F.count("*").alias(...)` → `COUNT(*) AS order_count`; `F.when(...).otherwise(...)` → `CASE WHEN ... END`; `.cast("timestamp")` → `CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP)`; `df.filter(...)` → `WHERE state = 'NY'`.

sql.explain_extra: In SQL these are table functions and expressions that you write inside a `SELECT`.

pairs.right: Reads files from a Volume as a table, without creating a table first
Converts text to a timestamp and fails on text it cannot convert
Converts text to a timestamp and returns NULL when it cannot

pairs.left: CASE WHEN year(registration_date) >= 2025 THEN 'New' ELSE 'Loyal' END
pairs.right: Picks a value by condition; the first matching branch wins
Counts rows (per group with GROUP BY) and names the result column
Path of the file each row was read from

hints: Read each expression out loud: the function names say what they do (`read_files`, `CAST`, `COUNT`).
`try_cast` is the forgiving twin of `CAST`: same conversion, but NULL instead of an error. `_metadata` is a hidden column that describes the source file.

Pairs: `read_files(...)` → reads files as a table; `CAST(...)` → converts or fails; `try_cast(...)` → converts or returns NULL; `CASE WHEN ... END` → value by condition; `COUNT(*) AS order_count` → counts rows; `_metadata.file_path` → path of the source file.
sql.solution:
read_files('/Volumes/<catalog>/default/datasets/customers/customers.csv', format => 'csv')  ->  Reads files from a Volume as a table, without creating a table first
CAST(order_datetime AS TIMESTAMP)  ->  Converts text to a timestamp and fails on text it cannot convert
try_cast(order_datetime AS TIMESTAMP)  ->  Converts text to a timestamp and returns NULL when it cannot
CASE WHEN year(registration_date) >= 2025 THEN 'New' ELSE 'Loyal' END  ->  Picks a value by condition; the first matching branch wins
COUNT(*) AS order_count  ->  Counts rows (per group with GROUP BY) and names the result column
_metadata.file_path  ->  Path of the file each row was read from

pyspark.explain_extra: The setup cell runs `from pyspark.sql import functions as F`. `F` holds the functions you know from SQL: `F.year` is `year()`, `F.count` is `COUNT`, `F.when` is `CASE WHEN`. Keeping them under `F` means Python's own `sum()` or `max()` keep working. Match each PySpark expression with the SQL that does the same thing.

pairs.right: CASE WHEN cond THEN 'New' ELSE 'Loyal' END

hints: Read the PySpark side as SQL: the function name usually stays the same (`year` → `year`, `count` → `COUNT`).
`.alias(...)` is SQL `AS`, `.otherwise(...)` is `ELSE`, and `.filter(...)` becomes a `WHERE` clause.

Pairs: `F.col("city")` → `city`; `F.year(...)` → `year(registration_date)`; `F.count("*").alias(...)` → `COUNT(*) AS order_count`; `F.when(...).otherwise(...)` → `CASE WHEN ... END`; `.cast("timestamp")` → `CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP)`; `df.filter(...)` → `WHERE state = 'NY'`.
pyspark.solution:
F.col("city")  ->  city (a column reference)
F.year(F.col("registration_date"))  ->  year(registration_date)
F.count("*").alias("order_count")  ->  COUNT(*) AS order_count
F.when(cond, "New").otherwise("Loyal")  ->  CASE WHEN cond THEN 'New' ELSE 'Loyal' END
F.col("order_datetime").cast("timestamp")  ->  CAST(order_datetime AS TIMESTAMP)
df.filter(F.col("state") == "NY")  ->  WHERE state = 'NY'

steps.title: Load CSV with an inferred schema
steps.explain: A raw file has no table yet: you read it straight from your Volume. The first row of `customers.csv` holds the column names (the `header` option), and Spark can scan the file to guess the column types (schema inference), which costs an extra pass over the data. Put the blocks in order; two blocks are not needed.

blocks.code:
.option("header", "true")        # first row = column names
    .option("inferSchema", "true")   # let Spark guess the types

hints: A read always starts with `spark.read` and ends with `.load(path)`. Writing (`.write`, `.saveAsTable`) does not belong here.
Order: assignment with `(`, `spark.read.format("csv")`, the options block (both `.option(...)` lines), `.load(CUSTOMERS_CSV)`, `)`, then `display(...)`.

Full solution:
```python
customers_infer_df = (
    spark.read.format("csv")
    .option("header", "true")        # first row = column names
    .option("inferSchema", "true")   # let Spark guess the types
    .load(CUSTOMERS_CSV)
)
display(customers_infer_df.limit(5))
```

blocks.code: CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW customers_infer AS

format => 'csv',
  header => true      -- first row = column names

sql.explain_extra: `read_files(...)` reads the file as a table inside `FROM`; `format => 'csv'` and `header => true` are named arguments. It infers the column types by default and adds a `_rescued_data` column for values that do not fit them. `CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW` names the result for the next statements of your session; no data is copied. Replace `<catalog>` in the path with your catalog name.
hints: A query reads `FROM` a source; here the source is the table function `read_files(...)`: the path first, then the options. Nothing is inserted.
Order: `CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW customers_infer AS`, `SELECT *`, `FROM read_files(`, the path, the options, `);`, then the preview with `LIMIT 5`.

Full solution:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW customers_infer AS
SELECT *
FROM read_files(
  '/Volumes/<catalog>/default/datasets/customers/customers.csv',
  format => 'csv',
  header => true      -- first row = column names
);
SELECT * FROM customers_infer LIMIT 5;
```

steps.title: Load CSV with an explicit schema
steps.explain: An explicit schema is the column list you would write in `CREATE TABLE`: `customer_id STRING, first_name STRING, ...`. With it Spark skips the extra scan and you control every type. CSV columns are matched by position, so the order must follow the file. `registration_date` is in `YYYY-MM-DD` format, so `DATE` parses it directly.
steps.expected: 10 columns in the CSV order, `registration_date` as DATE, the rest STRING; 10,000 rows.
steps.template:
# Schema as a DDL string: 10 columns in the CSV order
customers_schema = (
    "customer_id STRING, first_name STRING, last_name STRING, email STRING, phone STRING, "
    "city STRING, state STRING, country STRING, registration_date {{b1}}, customer_segment STRING"
)

# Load the CSV with the explicit schema (no inferSchema)
customers_df = (
    spark.read
    .format("csv")
    .option("{{b2}}", "true")
    .{{b3}}(customers_schema)
    .load({{b4}})
)
display(customers_df.limit(5))

# saves your result so the app can check it
customers_df.write.mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{CATALOG}.default._ws_ws_ingestion_t03")

steps.title: Explore the customer data
steps.explain: Before transforming data, look at it: how many rows there are and how many distinct values a column has. All customers are from the USA, so `country` has one distinct value.
steps.starter:

# total_rows         = number of rows in customers_df (int)
# distinct_countries = number of distinct values in country (int)
# summary_df         = summary statistics of customers_df (DataFrame)

# saves your result so the app can check it
(spark.createDataFrame([(total_rows, distinct_countries)], "total_rows BIGINT, distinct_countries BIGINT")
 .write.mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{CATALOG}.default._ws_ws_ingestion_t04"))
hints: Three separate one-liners on `customers_df`. Counting returns a Python `int`, `summary()` returns a DataFrame.
Pattern: `df.count()`, `df.select("col").distinct().count()`, `df.summary()`.

distinct_countries = customers_df.select("country").distinct().count()

 .write.mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{CATALOG}.default._ws_ws_ingestion_t04"))

steps.title: Filter customers
steps.explain: A filter keeps the rows where a condition is true, like SQL `WHERE`. `IN (...)` matches a list of values, and `year(registration_date)` takes the year of a date.
steps.expected: Customers from NY or CA: only those two states (about 1,600 rows). Customers registered in 2025 or later: no row before 2025.
steps.starter:
# Step 06 — your code
# customers_ny_ca  = customers from the states NY or CA
# customers_recent = customers registered in 2025 or later (PySpark or spark.sql)

# saves your result so the app can check it
(customers_ny_ca.withColumn("_part", F.lit("ny_ca")).unionByName(customers_recent.withColumn("_part", F.lit("recent")), allowMissingColumns=True)
 .write.mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{CATALOG}.default._ws_ws_ingestion_t06"))
hints: Two `filter` calls on `customers_df`, or one of them as `spark.sql("SELECT ... FROM customers_view WHERE ...")`.
Building blocks: `F.col("state").isin([...])` and `F.year(F.col("registration_date")) >= 2025`.

Full solution:
```python
# Step 06 — PySpark filter with isin
customers_ny_ca = customers_df.filter(F.col("state").isin(["NY", "CA"]))

# SQL option on the temp view (PySpark: F.year(F.col("registration_date")) >= 2025)
customers_recent = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM customers_view WHERE year(registration_date) >= 2025")

print(f"NY or CA: {customers_ny_ca.count():,} | recent: {customers_recent.count():,}")

# saves your result so the app can check it
(customers_ny_ca.withColumn("_part", F.lit("ny_ca")).unionByName(customers_recent.withColumn("_part", F.lit("recent")), allowMissingColumns=True)
 .write.mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").saveAsTable(f"{CATALOG}.default._ws_ws_ingestion_t06"))
```

steps.title: Add columns and cast types
steps.explain: New columns are expressions over existing ones. `concat_ws(' ', a, b)` joins strings with a separator and skips NULL. Casting to TIMESTAMP converts text such as `2024-12-31T23:56:00`; NULL stays NULL. If a text value cannot be converted, Databricks raises an error; `try_cast` returns NULL instead.
steps.expected: Customers get `full_name` (STRING) and `registration_year` (INT); orders get `order_ts` (TIMESTAMP) with no new NULLs.
steps.template:
# customers_enriched: full_name and registration_year
customers_enriched = (
    customers_df
    .{{b1}}("full_name", F.concat_ws({{b2}}, F.col("first_name"), F.col("last_name")))
    .withColumn("registration_year", F.{{b3}}(F.col("registration_date")))
)

# orders_typed: order_datetime (STRING) cast to TIMESTAMP

SELECT order_id, customer_id, first_name, last_name, country, total_amount, payment_method
FROM orders_view
LEFT JOIN customers_view USING (customer_id);

SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(total_amount) AS total_revenue
FROM orders_enriched

ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

sql.intro: SQL track: you query the files directly with `read_files(...)` and keep the intermediate results as temporary views (`customers_view`, `orders_view`, ...). To run the code, use `%sql` cells in `WORKSHOP_ingestion` after its setup cells, or the SQL editor after `USE CATALOG <catalog>;`. Replace `<catalog>` in the paths with your catalog name (`retailhub_<your login>`). A temporary view lives only in its session, so run the steps in order in the same notebook or editor tab.
